title: Is investing in art worth in this AI age?
author: Free-Version-2746
selftext:
Say need 2 months to dev a game. Now it will need another 5 months to make all assets your own.

Do you thing it is worth? Or take that 5 months to polish gameplays better choice.

comments.author: CharacterTension2896
comments.body: You know I tried making assets many ways. Now I tell it to use Blender and put it on a quality loop with a Qa and visual check to critique and it’s been ok. On the next occasion I wanna start with it making a fully featured game engine for the game. Also, I’ve seen GitHub have some free ways to get assets in. I’ll loop that into the game engine also.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body:
I have found this is the best way. These LLMs are not visual models, they understand math and angles and geometry but they don’t really have vision. So pixel art and keeping characters consistent through animations and making it look natural I think is hard for them. But rendering a 3d model especially simpler low poly ones seems to come more naturally. I have had it generate more machine related assets and it seems to do quite a good job with it

A lot of issues and the “AI” look I’ve noticed are when people try to make it do smooth pixel art or sprite type animations

comments.author: RageshAntony
comments.body:
If everybody can make burger, why we need to start a restaurant ? 

Art comes from sentient mind filled with consciousness and  conscience. Until AI gets this, it can't produce a quality art.

comments.author: Sencha-Games
comments.body: AI art looks like shit at the moment so I think it's worth investing in either learning art or hiring artists if you want to make something good.

comments.author: Significant-Neck-520
comments.body:
AI is much better for producing the code than it is for producing the assets. The code seems to be very good, while the art, even if impressive, is not up to par with professional work. 

 Maybe it could change in the future, but currently I still think producing the art is worth it, if you have the skills

replies.author: Limp_Bus3865
replies.body: It is not, and you explained why. Because it will soon be on human level

replies.author: TopTippityTop
replies.body:
The issue isn't the rendering, it's the taste, understanding of context, understanding of how design connects and how it all ties with the whole. AI, be it llms or generative image models, are terrible at this. They have not improved. 

So long as that is the case, they will not be at human level where it counts, and will remain tools.

replies.author: Limp_Bus3865
replies.body: they are not good at this YET. Jesus the amount of time I heard "ai is terrible at this" and then they publish AI that can do that perfectly in two weeks

replies.author: Alternative-Bread411
replies.body:
I'm not even saying AI is bad. It's good enough in some cases, but in saturated markets, good enough gets lost. AI is fundamentally derivative, which makes it an amazing tool for legwork, but that comes with creative limitations. There's a difference between replicating the appearance of art and having the taste, intent and personal perspective behind it.

I'm not knocking AI. I use it myself. It's just not a silver bullet for creativity or artistic expression.

replies.author: TMiyoshi
replies.body:
I've been hearing that it's gonna be good soon, for 3 years though.

It's getting better but it still has basic issues because the funding and training is going into your mom generating cat videos and not developers generating consistent artstyles.

replies.author: Alternative-Bread411
replies.body:
I think this idea that AI is inevitably going to become a silver bullet for creativity in X years is both unrealistic and a bit depressing.

Of course it'll improve technically, but technical capability isn't the same as creativity or artistic expression. Personally, I'd much rather see AI evolve into a tool that empowers artists rather than one that attempts to replace them. Let it handle the grunt work so humans can focus on the creative stuff.

replies.author: Limp_Bus3865
replies.body: I hope you are right, but we will see. There has to be a limit to what ai can do at some point

replies.author: TopTippityTop
replies.body:
Yes, yet. 

We've basically seen no improvement in any of these areas, really. 

If you tell it to do something good, it will. It doesn't know what good is, and it doesn't find it on its own.
When I see it improving, then it'll be a matter of time.

This is the difference between a mediocre and generic motion graphics animation woth Opus 5.5, and one that looks amazing.

People make skills to try and improve it, by giving it some direction, but you still need to feed it references. Why good references? Because humans with good taste made them. Scale that supply by 100x, as AI will do, and suddenly finding great reference is rare. Your own good taste will remain relevant and important.

No matter how intelligent it is, its  understanding of human experience stops at words. Yet you feel it. You know what being human feels like. What it feels like to experience mundane things such as the color of a hot-dog package. You may find that irrelevant, but it is relevant in logo making, marketing, package design, etc. It just understands the words, which are distilled from our experience. It gets it close, but not all the way. No matter how intelligent, it will lack in experience.

That is what we bring to the table. I work with it professionally, I've trained models and Lora, it's my daily life. It's quite obvious to me where it lacks, and it has little to do with intelligence.

replies.author: Alternative-Bread411
replies.body:
I doubt it will ever be on a human level, because art is fundamentally human expression. There's a stark difference between visual quality and artistic expression.

It's like comparing a three chord pop song to a complex classical composition. Just because something is technically more sophisticated doesn't mean it'll resonate more with an audience.

Art isn't simply a measure of technical quality.

replies.author: Limp_Bus3865
replies.body: so you are telling me that 90% of music that makes money in todays world is not a four chord pop aong but a classical composition? who are you trying to deceive? me or yourself?

replies.author: Alternative-Bread411
replies.body: Haha, you've completely misunderstood my point. That's exactly what I'm saying! Technical complexity doesn't equal artistic quality or audience appeal. A simple four chord pop song can resonate more than an incredibly sophisticated classical composition. That's the entire point of the analogy. It’s unpredictable and human.

replies.author: Condurum
replies.body:
Even if it was, most ai users would screw it up by taking bad decisions, I guarantee it. 

Ex Art Director in games here. People without great taste consistently choose the worst solution.

replies.author: Alternative-Bread411
replies.body:
I wholeheartedly agree. I see a lot of artists worried about AI replacing them, but I actually think the opposite. The very way AI is built and operates it have huge fundamental creative limitations.

I'm not an AI hater, quite the opposite. I think it's a fantastic tool for speeding up production, but people massively underestimate the taste, design, intent and communication that goes into creating art.

In games especially, there's another layer of gameplay readability. Art isn't just about making something look good, it's about making deliberate creative decisions that serve the experience.

comments.author: PersonalityOk5729
comments.body: I think for normal quality it's sufficient if you *work* with Ai instead of just try to one shot assets. Artists are incredibly expensive and understand you less than AI and you'll need very, very experienced and expensive artists if you want quality work

comments.author: WolfedUpLlama
comments.body:
Adding the general public is more forgiving and or blissful to AI-coded projects compared to AI visuals. (I’m a motion designer in advertising for context)

Same thing from what I’ve seen in the book community. Readers tend to despise books written by AI.

Guess the way I look at it is if there 100 people willing to buy a game and 40 do not want AI visuals, you’ve cut your chances to 60 people compared to none AI visuals, i can’t imagine there are pro AI people who aren’t going to play a game that doesn’t us actually visuals made from a human.

comments.author: Kiran__reddit
comments.body: if you love art absolutely, Games are one of human's best creation.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
yes but it is "art direction", "art taste" (basically design) and not "how to use this custom brush to do easy shading" or "this one layer trick will simplify your workflow" etc

I have been reviewing AI games and I can tell you that people with a design background stand out pretty well. 

On the other hand, devs with a tech background (you can guess which group I belong to) tend to make similar mistakes: has poor color choices like they are color blind, mishandling pixel art because "close enough" etc

so AI devs with art/design background are eating well rn

I am not sure how one grinds "design" but that is what you need to stand out

comments.author: Apalala__
comments.body:
the stronger you are at defining art terms and techniques,  
the better you reason out to AI how to create specific things.

comments.author: Xanma_6aki
comments.body: Making asset does not take that long also while ai can make decent assets in 3d people hate it much more than they hate ai code for some reason

comments.author: EchoingAngel
comments.body: AI can do art, but there's quite a few limitations that you need to be aware of before you get too deep into how visuals/animations work in your game. Animations are rough, smooth surfaces are rough, and making coherent "families" are really hard currently. These things massively affected my design decisions. So don't spend too much time on a barebones game until you have an idea of what AI can get you

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
AI art, at best, is serviceable right now. I've been happy with a few pieces, but I know for a fact that if I could afford it, those same pieces would have been much better done by an artist.

If you can afford an artist, hire an artist. Period. The work will look better, and there are a huge number of benefits from that kind of collab that you will never get from the machine (example: the artist will also want to promote your game since their work is featured in it, so now you have multiple people in different social circles expanding the game's presence).

Also, 99% of the time - even with decent AI generations - the art still looks like AI art, because the machine has its own stylistic tendencies, and that's a major turn-off for most people (right now).

comments.author: Able_Zombie_7859
comments.body: Human made content will arguably become MORE valuable in the face of a torrent of ai content

comments.author: OakNLeaf
comments.body:
That's why you don't make the assets on your own. The problem with just letting AI do it is that you end up with AI slop. 

AI Slop makes it look like you don't care about your product regardless of how much time you have spent polishing your games features. 

My process is going to be to use AI for placeholders (I haven't started the prototype process yet) using a Style Guide I created and then when I get a art style I like I will pay Artist to help create the Art. 

Obviously that's my own process, I don't expect anyone else to do it, but I want to have as little AI facing the actual user I can, so anything UI/text based that is visible to the user I want an actual human to make.

replies.author: Ashamed-Cost-5548
replies.body: better yet, let the artist make the art direction based on your creative directuon. open up tourself to artist feedback becausethe best looking game have the best art director. and that takes nothing from you

comments.author: GameNotFound
comments.body: In this current climate, you mention AI and people will riot (and not necessarily for bad reason). This should also be considered when contemplating integrating AI into your work flow.

comments.author: q_OwO_p
comments.body: It’s only worth investing if you learn to make art yourself because it’s a highly rewarding thing to do so

comments.author: ItsDumi
comments.body: For me, what i enjoy about art is the process where designing a character feels more like building an imaginary place with rules and history and having the skill to output exactly what I imagine is v nice and helpful. If you did it passively for 5 years you'd only benefit from doing it

comments.author: TopTippityTop
comments.body: Invest in art vision, someone with great taste and direction who's willing to use the tools. That's worth it.

comments.author: Alternative-Bread411
comments.body:
Yes! If there's one area I'd invest in, not just in games but any product in an AI-saturated market, it's the consumer facing. Particularly visuals, but also animation and audio.

AI is an incredibly powerful tool, but when it comes to art, it often produces something familiar. In an increasingly competitive market, familiar isn't good enough.

Artists bring their own taste, experiences and vision to their work, which is what makes it distinctive. They also have far greater control and consistency over their output. AI can produce something stunning once, but maintaining that quality across an entire project is another matter.

As AI makes creating things easier, I think strong artistic identity will only become more valuable.

comments.author: CubersumGame
comments.body:
The question is: what for?

If you need to make money quickly, AI can help.

If you want to draw for self-expression, you learn to draw.

It’s like with clothing. If you just need something to wear, you buy clothes at a store - yet millions of people still sew and knit.

comments.author: monsterfurby
comments.body: Art and voice acting (and technically music, but that's often prohibitively expensive) are two areas I think hiring a human is not just ethically right, but also leads to way better results. Not every asset probably, but key art, and depending on the art style also in-game art.

comments.author: wgzz
comments.body:
You wna make a good looking game, then yes. Get an artist.

You wna make a 💩 looking slop, then go gen it
